metadata.title: Bridging the Pixel Gap in Browser Automation.
metadata.purpose: Teardown-register recut of the coordinate-scaling explainer: take apart why Claude's click coordinate lands in the wrong place, name the design choice that put it there (fixed model input surface), and show the multiply-back fix.
metadata.anchor_pair: B01 -> B04 (same rectangle pair, same button)
metadata.one_flag: none — fully sourced from coordinate_scaling.py, see SOURCES.md

beats.narration_text: Ciao, Liam — in for Bear. Claude reports a click at 728, 364. Here's what's actually happening: that number was never measured on your screen. It was measured on a resized copy of it. Why does the pipeline hand you a coordinate from a different picture, and what does that choice cost you?

beats.narration_text: Here's the mechanism. Claude never touches your real screen. Before the model looks at anything, your screenshot gets squeezed to a fixed 1456 by 819 pixels — that is the model's input surface, always, for 16:9. Your viewport is 1920 by 1080. Two coordinate spaces, one button. They optimized for a predictable input size at the expense of matching your screen.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — two rectangles, 1456x819 and 1920x1080, same button dot at different relative positions, bridged by a question mark

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — two spaces, one button
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Left rectangle labelled '1456 × 819 — what Claude sees' with a terracotta button dot. Right rectangle labelled '1920 × 1080 — your real screen', larger, same aspect. A question-mark arrow bridges them. THIS EXACT PAIR OF RECTANGLES RETURNS AT B04.

beats.narration_text: The obvious move is to take Claude's number and click it — 728, 364, done. Do that and you miss, cleanly. The button never sat at 728, 364 on your 1920 by 1080 screen; that was its position inside the smaller picture the model was looking at. You're clicking the right coordinate in the wrong coordinate system.

shot.new_visual_element: Same anchor pair; raw (728,364) carried straight across onto the 1920x1080 rectangle — misses the button, struck

production_viz.label: Same raw pixel, wrong canvas
production_viz.mechanic: The B01 rectangle pair returns. The (728, 364) dot is carried across unscaled onto the 1920×1080 rectangle; it lands short of a target ring near center, marked with a cross. Caption: 'nowhere close to the button'.

beats.narration_text: The fix is the inverse of the resize. Whatever ratio squeezed your screen down to 1456 by 819 is exactly what you multiply back — 1920 over 1456 for x, 1080 over 819 for y, both about 1.32. Multiply Claude's number by that, clamp it inside your screen so a rounding error can't fire an off-canvas click, and you have the real coordinate.

shot.new_visual_element: Formula card: real_x = x * (viewport_w / 1456), real_y = y * (viewport_h / 819), then a clamp note; source credit

production_viz.label: The inverse ratio
production_viz.mechanic: Two formula lines build in ink mono on cream: 'real_x = x × (viewport_w / 1456)' then 'real_y = y × (viewport_h / 819)'. Beneath, a smaller terracotta line: 'clamp to [0, viewport_w-1] / [0, viewport_h-1]'. Caption bottom-right: 'Source: Claude Quickstarts (Anthropic)'.

beats.narration_text: Run the numbers. 728 times 1920 over 1456 is 960. 364 by the same ratio is 480. Click 960, 480 — it lands, exactly on the button. That math is only right for the 16:9 case, because 1456 by 819 is a lookup, not a formula. Feed Claude a different aspect ratio and it resizes to a different fixed size — new target dimensions, new ratio, same multiply-back move. The mechanism is a table plus a multiplication; the table is what the API decided your screen looks like.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — same rectangle pair, dot now scaled and lands on target; a third non-16:9 rectangle beside it, struck, captioned 'different lookup table'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — scaled, and it lands
production_viz.mechanic: THE B01/B02 RECTANGLE PAIR RETURNS, identical. This time (728, 364) is carried across with the ratio applied, landing exactly on the target ring at '(960, 480)' inside the 1920×1080 rectangle, marked with a check. Off to the side, a third, differently-proportioned rectangle appears, struck through, captioned 'not 16:9 — different table' — the caveat, not the main case.

beats.narration_text: A Claude coordinate isn't wrong. It's measured on a smaller picture. Multiply back by the resize ratio, and the click lands where you meant it to.

props.quote: A Claude coordinate isn't wrong — it's just measured on a smaller picture. Multiply back by the resize ratio, and the click lands exactly where you meant.
props.sparkLine: Resized picture, not a wrong number.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — my model clicks at 700, 410 on a 1456 by 819 screenshot, but my screen is 1920 by 1080; write the scaling function and land the click exactly. Go deeper: ask what breaks the moment the aspect ratio isn't 16 by 9, and how the multiply-back move has to change. Liam, in for Bear.

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm using Claude's computer-use tool. It just returned a click coordinate of (700, 410), but its screenshot is 1456×819 pixels and my real viewport is 1920×1080 pixels. Write a Python function `to_real(x, y, viewport_w, viewport_h, model_w=1456, model_h=819)` that scales the model coordinate back into the real viewport, clamps to [0, viewport_w-1] and [0, viewport_h-1] so a rounding error can't fire an off-canvas click, and returns integers. Show the function, run it on (700, 410) with my viewport, and print the resulting real (x, y). Then explain in one paragraph what the ratio means physically and why the clamp is not optional.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: what happens the moment my viewport isn't 16:9? Claude resizes non-16:9 screenshots to a different fixed size — find that size, work out the new ratio, and modify the function so it picks the correct lookup entry from the viewport's aspect ratio instead of assuming 1456×819.
